results.content:
Yes, EV battery cells and packs from China face Section 301 tariffs of 25% on top of the base 3.4% duty. This has accelerated battery production shifts to South Korea, Japan, and domestic US facilities.

### What HTS code is used for batteries?

Batteries fall under HTS 8507 (electric accumulators). Lithium-ion is 8507.60, lead-acid is 8507.10, nickel-metal hydride is 8507.50. Each has different base duty rates ranging from 2.7% to 3.4%.

The U.S. Customs & Border Protection (CBP) published a Notice that would revoke the Agency’s previous rulings on lithium ion cells in favor of classifying cells in the U.S. harmonized tariff schedule (HTS) applicable to batteries. Until 2018, the CBP’s tariff classification position on cells and batteries was of little practical importance because there was no difference in the duties applicable to imports under any of the applicable codes. However, the CBP’s stance took on heightened [...] took on heightened importance beginning in 2018, when the first Trump Administration imposed additional tariffs of 25% on Chinese lithium ion battery parts while imposing lower additional duties of 7.5% on Chinese lithium ion batteries. results.title: HS Code for Batteries (US) | Gaia Dynamics
results.content:
Batteries are split between two HTS headings: 8506 covers \\primary\\ (non-rechargeable) batteries (alkaline, lithium primary, manganese dioxide), and 8507 covers \\secondary\\ (rechargeable) batteries: lead-acid, nickel-metal hydride, lithium-ion, and others. Lithium-ion batteries (8507.60) are the most economically significant subheading because they cover laptops, phones, EV traction packs, power tools, and grid storage. General MFN rates range from 2.5% to 3.5% across the heading. Battery [...] The \\lithium-ion EV vs other split\\ at 8507.60.00.10 vs.20 matters for both rate (same 3.4% MFN, but Section 301 stacking differs) and statistical reporting under recent EV-related trade measures.

A practical note: batteries integrated into a finished device (a laptop with a built-in battery, a power tool with a battery pack) generally follow the parent device's classification. Standalone batteries (including OEM replacements and aftermarket packs) classify under 8506 / 8507. [...] | HTS Code | Description | Duty Rate |

results.content:
If you are having trouble logging in, please

by Descartes Datamyne | Sep 17, 2015 | Imports, Indicators

Yet another sign that electric cars are catching on: A new 10-digit Harmonized Tariff System code has been established for the lithium-ion batteries used to power electrical vehicles: HS 8507.60.0010. Until now, the HS codes did not distinguish between EV batteries and Li-Ion batteries used in consumer electronic devices and power tools. [...] Ironically, the electric vehicles these Li-Ion batteries power are yet to be given their own HS code. EVs are covered by the all-purpose “Motor Vehicles – Other” code of HS 8703.90.00. The World Customs Organization has proposed a separate code for EVs as part of the next round of HS revisions in 2017. Look for the US to adopt the revised codes – and for more precise data on trade in EVs – a year earlier, in 2016.

Related: [...] The code became effective in July – and July’s US trade data, the first to capture imports of EV-purposed Li-Ion batteries, was released earlier this month:

The trade data captured by the new HS code for Tesla and other EV makers fits with other information pieced together by market watchers.

results.title: Battery Pack Tariffs: What OEMs Need to Know in 2026
results.content:
Chinese lithium-ion cells are subject to a 30 percent baseline tariff under the current trade policy framework. This is layered on top of existing Section 301 tariffs that apply to battery products. Additionally, if the cells use Chinese graphite in the anode – which most globally manufactured cells do – the 93.5 percent graphite tariff is embedded in the cell cost before it reaches the US border. The effective tariff burden on Chinese-origin cells is therefore substantially higher than the 30 [...] Multiple tariff measures took effect simultaneously. A 93.5 percent tariff on Chinese graphite – the primary anode material in virtually all lithium-ion batteries – took effect, representing one of the most significant raw material tariffs in US manufacturing history. A 30 percent baseline tariff on all Chinese goods compounded the impact on battery cells and pack components sourced from China. Steel and copper tariffs of 50 percent added further cost pressure on pack housings, connectors, [...] Full BOM tariff audit completed with HTS codes and country of origin for all components
 Cell source country of origin documented and tariff exposure quantified
 Graphite anode origin traced and Chinese graphite tariff exposure assessed

 Alternative cell sources qualified or qualification plan established

results.title: The Tariff Tangle: China Trade & the Battery Industry in 2025
results.content: Graphite is a crucial raw material for EV batteries, accounting for approximately 10% of the cell cost in Lithium-Ion batteries. This substantial tariff is expected to significantly raise the cost of building EVs at American plants, negatively impacting the automotive industry. While domestic graphite producers believe it will help increase investment and production in the domestic industry, the US industry does not currently produce enough high-purity graphite needed for EV batteries (99.9% [...] By August 2025, the landscape had evolved further, particularly for electric vehicle (EV) batteries. For EV lithium-ion batteries, the combined tariff rate has increased from 7.5% to 58% in 2025. Some analyses suggest that the total tariffs could be as high as 173% for EV batteries and 156% for non-EV batteries. While a temporary “tariff truce” may be in effect today, these underlying higher rates remain a significant factor for the industry. [...] EV batteries (99.9% carbon purity). Attorneys for automakers, including Tesla, have argued that US producers are not able to produce graphite to these exacting specifications, making immediate supply switching difficult. It will take time for the domestic market to catch up, meaning domestic battery makers will likely just have to pay higher prices for Chinese graphite in the interim. Furthermore, the Section 301 tariff on natural graphite is specifically scheduled to increase to 25% by January
